summary: After 3 iterations, the problem is solved at the maximum possible score of 100/100. The algorithm sorts a permutation using prefix-suffix swap operations in ~1987 operations on average (worst case 1993 observed, theoretical bound 1996), well under the scoring threshold of 2001. No further score improvement is possible due to the judge's clamping mechanism.
key_points: Score 100/100 achieved on all 10 judge test cases across iterations 1-3; the judge clamps scores at 100, so this is the ceiling — no further improvement is possible.

The algorithm places elements into sorted order using a circular-buffer rotation technique (2 operations per element), with a k=4 endgame optimization that handles the last 4 elements in ≤4 operations via precomputed BFS-optimal sequences. Total worst-case: 2n-4 = 1996 operations for n=1000.
Observed operation counts on judge test cases: min=1984, max=1993, avg=1987.3. Validated on 200 additional random n=1000 permutations with 0 failures (min=1971, max=1993, avg=1983.5).

Alternative approaches exhaustively analyzed and ruled out: k=5 endgame (computationally intractable), batch placement (negligible savings for random permutations), reverse selection sort, cycle-based methods, and single-operation placement all proven equal or inferior to the 2-ops-per-element bound.

Continuing further iterations has no expected value for the scored metric. Potential academic extensions (k=5 endgame via C++ BFS, formal lower bounds, generalization to related operations) would not change the score. Recommend approving campaign completion.
